newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain embraces labour reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Spain embraces labour reform plans.

text.p: The Spanish government on Tuesday embraced labour reform plans struck between employers and unions and said it would put the reforms into practice as swiftly as possible.

Unions and employers finished drafting a deal on Monday after months of intensive talks. The two sides said their executive bodies must still ratify the agreement, although it is widely expected to win overwhelming approval.

"The reforms are good news and put us among the foremost European countries in terms of social stability....the government intends to put the reforms into practice as soon as possible," Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told reporters.

The government hopes the reforms will go part of the way toward liberalising Spain's highly rigid labour market and suppressing its towering unemployment -- the highest in Europe at just under 22 percent.
Unions and employers reached a preliminary agreement in March that provided the foundations for a final accord, and have been putting the agreement down on paper since then.

The two sides said they would reveal the details of the draft on Wednesday after tying up any loose ends. It will then be presented to their executive committees for approval later in April and could be signed by the end of the month.

The key feature of the accord is a permanent contract which allows for cheaper severance pay in cases where dismissal could be judged unfair -- 33 days pay per year worked with a maximum of 24 months.
Unions are optimistic that this new contract will encourage employers to stop abusing temporary contracts which accounted for 96 percent of new jobs created in 1996, according to the Labour Ministry.
"(The deal) constitutes a mortal blow to job insecurity," said UGT spokesman Antonio Ordonez. "This will be a very balanced instrument if put to use."
Employers have complained that Spain's high dismissal costs dissuaded them from taking on staff under permanent contracts.

The accord also details a new permanent contract aimed at young people between 18 and 29 years, long-term unemployed, older workers and the handicapped. The incentives given to employers to use this new contract are as yet unknown.
The types of contracts available will be reduced and clarified and a new contract for training and college leavers will be created.
The accord also aims to clarify the reasons that an employer can give for redundancies. In the case of fair dismissals, an employer must only pay severance costs of 20 days per year worked.
The employers' association CEOE said it would present the deal for approval by its board of directors on April 15. The unions said their regional leaders would vote on April 22.
The General Workers' Union (UGT) said the deal could be signed on April 25.
